units.title: 3.1 Government and politics of the UK

outcomes.text: Know the scope of UK government and politics.
Understand how the UK is governed.
Define codified and uncodified constitutions, statute, common law, conventions, royal prerogative, rule of law and parliamentary sovereignty.
Know how Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights, the Act of Settlement and the Parliament Acts shaped UK rights.
Evaluate the nature and sources of the British constitution and debates on the extent of rights.
Evaluate two constitutional changes since 1997 (devolution, Freedom of Information, Human Rights Act, Lords reform).
Analyse where individual and collective rights agree and conflict.
Explain scrutiny of the executive, the Commons and Lords, and the legislative process.
Compare Burkean, delegate and mandate theories of representation.
Evaluate the roles and influence of MPs and peers, committees and the opposition.
Evaluate Parliament's influence on government: party discipline, civil servants and Select Committees, Whips.
Analyse interactions between Parliament and other branches.
Define the core executive, primus inter pares, cabinet, cabinet committees, and collective and individual responsibility.
Evaluate policy making and the relationship between Prime Minister and cabinet.
Distinguish individual from collective responsibility using examples such as Crichel Down.
Analyse two examples of prime ministerial and cabinet power, one from 1945-97 and one since 1997.
Define the Supreme Court, judicial independence, separation of powers, ultra vires and judicial review.
Evaluate judicial composition and appointments.
Evaluate the Supreme Court's impact on government, legislature and policy, including judicial review.
Describe the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland bodies and their powers.
Evaluate devolution debates in England and existing English devolution.
Evaluate the impact of devolution on UK government.
Understand UK politics.
Define direct and representative democracy, suffrage, participation and partisan dealignment.
Describe how suffrage has changed since the Great Reform Act and debates over gender, class, ethnicity and age.
Explain the significance of the Chartists, Suffragists and Suffragettes, and suffrage as a human right.
Evaluate types of democracy and patterns and forms of participation.
Compare majoritarian and proportional systems in Westminster and one devolved body.
Evaluate advantages, disadvantages and performance debates of those systems.
Study three elections since 1945, including 1997: voting behaviour, media, policies, manifestos, campaigns, leadership and electoral system effects.
Evaluate the use and impact of referendums.
Explain the origins and development of the Conservative, Labour and Liberal Democrat parties and their current policies.
Evaluate party structures, functions and funding debates.
Evaluate party relations with the media and factors affecting outcomes.
Evaluate minor parties' influence and the move toward a multi-party system.
Define pluralism, insider and outsider groups, and promotional and interest groups.
Evaluate pressure groups and democracy, and influences such as think tanks, lobbyists, corporations and media.
Study one insider and one outsider group; evaluate methods and factors of influence, and links to parties, government and media.
Know EU institutions.
Evaluate EU aims and how far they were achieved, and its impact on UK politics and policy.

units.title: 3.2 Government and politics of the USA and comparative politics

topics.title: 3.2.1 Government and politics of the USA

outcomes.text: Know the scope of US and comparative politics.
Understand how the USA is governed.
Define the US Constitution, Bill of Rights, separation of powers, checks and balances and federalism.
Evaluate the Constitution's significance, framework, federal-state relations and amendment process.
Evaluate debates on the Constitution's importance today and the protection of civil liberties.
Define Congress, House, Senate, oversight and the committee system.
Evaluate Congress's structure, composition, terms and party allegiance.
Evaluate its legislative, oversight and purse powers and effectiveness.
Evaluate parties and committees, representative roles, the House versus Senate, and relations with the executive and Supreme Court.
Define formal and informal powers, imperial and imperilled presidency.
Evaluate sources of presidential power using two examples.
Distinguish formal powers (Article 2) from informal powers, including EXOP.
Evaluate constraints: checks and balances, party support in Congress, Supreme Court, media and public opinion.
Evaluate the president's relationship with cabinet, EXOP and bureaucracy, with an example of waxing and waning power, and the imperial versus imperilled debate.
Define judicial activism, restraint, judicial review and strict and loose constructionism.
Evaluate Supreme Court selection, appointment and composition.
Evaluate the Court as guardian of the Constitution and protector of rights, and the significance of judicial review.
Study two landmark rulings and the Court's role in shaping a policy area.
Define the electoral college, primaries, caucuses, conventions, direct democracy, split-ticket voting, abstention and incumbency.
Evaluate presidential and congressional elections, nomination and the electoral college.
Evaluate determinants of outcomes: money, media, issues, leadership, incumbency, and campaign finance debates.
Evaluate state-level direct democracy: referendums, initiatives, propositions and recall.
Evaluate US voting behaviour, party coalitions, realigning elections, split-ticket voting and abstention.
Define factionalism, party decline and renewal, party organisation, third parties and independents.
Evaluate the two main parties' ideologies, values, policies, traditions and organisation, and growing polarisation.
Evaluate factionalism, decline or renewal, party weakness, two-party dominance and third-party significance.
Define political pluralism, electoral finance, iron triangles, promotional and interest groups, PACs and Super PACs.
Evaluate US pluralism, typologies, methods and tactics.
Evaluate pressure group election funding, iron triangles, incumbency, power versus parties, and PACs and Super PACs.
Define civil liberties, Bill of Rights, landmark rulings and the Civil Rights movement.
Evaluate protection of rights under the Constitution, Bill of Rights, amendments and Supreme Court rulings.
Evaluate pressure groups' role in rights and the impact of one salient rights issue on US politics.
Compare UK and US politics.
Use structural, rational and cultural approaches to compare UK and US government.
Compare UK and US constitutions: codified or not, sources, separation of powers, checks and balances.
Compare UK devolution with US federalism.
Compare the legislatures' powers, composition, structure, strengths and weaknesses.
Compare the role, powers and accountability of the UK prime minister and US president.
Compare each leader's relationship to other institutions of government.
Compare the UK Supreme Court and US Supreme Court, their powers and bases.
Compare judicial independence and impact on government and politics.
Compare elections and electoral systems in the UK and USA.
Compare two-party and multi-party systems, and explain why the US has two parties.
Compare campaign and party finance debates, party unity, third parties and independents, and party policies.
Compare influences on government in the UK and USA.
Compare pressure groups' power, influence and methods.
Compare how civil rights are protected in the UK and USA.
Evaluate civil rights debates.
Compare methods, influence and effectiveness of civil rights campaigns.
Know the scope of political ideas.
Understand the core ideologies.
Explain liberal views on the individual, freedom, human nature, state, society and economy.
Distinguish classical from modern liberalism.
Study Locke, Mill, Rawls, T.H. Green, Wollstonecraft and Friedan on liberal thinking.
Explain conservative views on government, free market, individual, authority, tradition and property.
Distinguish traditional conservatism from the New Right.
Study Hobbes, Burke, Oakeshott, Rand and Nozick on conservative thinking.
Explain socialist views on Marxism, class analysis and fundamental goals.
Compare revolutionary socialism with social democracy.
Study Marx and Engels, Luxemburg, Webb, Crosland and Giddens on socialist thinking.
Understand one further ideology.
Explain nation and sovereignty of the people, with views on human nature, state, society and economy.
Compare minority and state nationalism and recent developments.
Study Rousseau, Herder, Mazzini, Garvey and Maurras on nationalism.
Explain equality of treatment, recognising gender differences and affirmative action.
Compare liberal and radical feminism, difference feminism and post-feminism.
Study Gilman, de Beauvoir, Millett, Rowbotham and hooks on feminism.
Explain equality of opportunity, anti-discrimination and assimilation.
Explain integration and segregation.
Study Berlin, Kymlicka, Taylor, Modood and Parekh on multiculturalism.
Explain individual autonomy, opposition to coercion and to government, and society without government.
Compare individualist and collectivist anarchist traditions.
Study Stirner, Bakunin, Goldman, Kropotkin and Proudhon on anarchism.
Explain the relationship between humankind and nature, and sustainability.
Distinguish light greens from dark greens.
Study Leopold, Carson, Schumacher, Merchant and Bookchin on ecologism.
